And feel free to reach out to us anytime at league@mlh.io.

articles.title: 926 Steps, Two Lobotomies, and Zero Nudges: Flight-Testing the Commitment Machine Across Gemini, Claude, and GPT-OSS
articles.description: A 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies found that AI agents write 30% more code and close zero additional tickets because review times jump 49%. Here is what happened when I put my 1986 Commitment Machine into live production across Gemini, Claude, and GPT-OSS.
articles.body_html:
A 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies found that AI coding agents write 30% more code and close zero extra tickets because PR review times jump 49%. When I ran my 1986 Commitment Machine across five live production tickets, a mid-flight vendor swap, and an open-weight crash test, here is what the flight recorder proved.

"The dashboard with the Mermaid state diagram is perfect. I find myself not even opening the pull requests now. I just wait for the green board or the triage details... And I also like that every code change is paired with an immediate critical reviewer. That one step really reduces friction."

— My notes to myself after the fourth ticket in a row

1. The Bottom Line Up Front: What Live Production Just Proved

Earlier this month, Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton published a massive study ("Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production", covered in Forkast News) tracking 718 companies and more than 725,000 software developers from 2021 to 2026.

By early 2026, over 95% of those companies had rolled out AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Devin). And the numbers they found should make every engineering manager wince:

  • Developers wrote +30% more code (1,500 extra lines per developer per month), and opened +23% more pull requests.
  • Yet the number of finished Jira tickets and epics went up by 0%.
  • Why? Because PR review wait times jumped +49% (+3.45 days), the number of PRs kicked back for rewrites nearly doubled, review comments per PR rose +35%, and 14% more senior engineers got dragged away from their own work to pay what the researchers call the "babysitting tax."

If you've ever worked on a real software team, you don't need an economics degree to spot the bug. If you make typing code 10x faster, but your AI never pushes back on a bad ticket and never catches its own bugs before committing, you haven't sped up your team. You've just aimed a firehose of plausible-looking slop at your senior reviewers.

In Part 3.10, I redesigned my coding workflow (Randal's Public Workflow Gist) specifically to invert that bottleneck—moving ticket pushback, adversarial code review, and state tracking before git commit using Fernando Flores's 1986 "Committed Speech" rules, a 1976 Makefile, and a 1983 /etc/init.d state directory (00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md).

Then I turned the key and ran five consecutive production tickets (926+ steps, 18 subagents), a 960-step mid-flight vendor swap, and a 791-step open-weight torture test through it.

Before we look at the flight logs, here is the bottom line from those runs:

  1. You beat the +30% code-bloat trap before writing a single line of code: When you force a read-only Codebase Archaeologist subagent to check a ticket's claims against git log before the agent is allowed to promise code, stale or already-solved tickets get closed in 8 minutes via a Counter-Offer (0 lines of code written) or trimmed in half—instead of turning into 300-line zombie PRs.
  2. You beat the +49% PR review bottleneck by running an Adversarial Critic before git commit and collapsing bot threads into one table: Pairing every code edit with a local Critic subagent and a single consolidated PR triage comment catches subtle framework bugs (like Flutter's post-await ScaffoldMessenger trap) locally, so the human reviewer doesn't even have to open the GitHub PR page until the board is green.
  3. Keeping state in /etc/init.d files on disk makes your agent both lobotomy-proof and vendor-agnostic: When every commitment lives in numbered Markdown files on disk instead of hidden inside one model's chat RAM, the agent not only survives back-to-back 200k-token context resets without losing its place—you can literally swap Claude Sonnet 4.6 for Gemini 4 at Step 433 of a 960-step run when a quota wall hits, and the new model finishes the job without missing a beat.
  4. External Makefile scaffolding has a hard floor—and a 120B open-weight model fell right through it: A Makefile can keep a capable model (Gemini 4 or Claude Sonnet 4.6) on the rails, but when I put GPT-OSS 120B into the exact same cockpit for 791 steps, it ignored the /etc/init.d files, suffered 6 context lobotomies, searched Google for private local Dart classes, and fork-bombed 6 simultaneous background git commit jobs while deleting .git/index.lock.

2. Why These Five Tickets Matter: Every One of Them Tests a Different Failure Mode

I didn't cherry-pick five easy toy problems. These were simply the next five tickets sitting in our production monorepo backlog—and each one happened to test a specific failure mode where normal AI coding agents create work instead of finishing it:

Ticket & The Failure Mode It Tested Steps / Subagents Context Resets What the Commitment Machine Did Differently Dev Nudges
1. TICKET-553: The Stale / Contradicted Ticket
(Tests whether the agent blindly writes +30% dead code on an obsolete ticket) 		69 steps
1 subagent		 0 Archaeologist proved the requested wrapper was already built and rejected in PR #927 two weeks ago. Issued a Counter-Offer: closed in 8m 29s with 0 lines of code. 0
2. TICKET-779: The Half-Solved Ticket
(Tests whether the agent re-implements work that already landed on main) 		135 steps
3 subagents		 0 Archaeologist proved the .scripts/*.sh pipefail guards had already landed in PR #1029, cutting the scope in half (AGENTS.md 31,248 / 32,000 byte cap only). 0
3. TICKET-482: The Linter Blind Spot & Bot Flood
(Tests whether subtle UI bugs and 14 bot threads get dumped on a human reviewer) 		189 steps
5 subagents		 2 Scoped 19 dialogs down to 15, caught a post-await ScaffoldMessenger bug (SCAR-RIV-14) that flutter analyze missed, and triaged 14 bot comments in 1 table. 0
4. TICKET-891: The Flaky Cloud CI Runner
(Tests whether a transient GitHub Actions hiccup drags a human back to babysit) 		182 steps
4 subagents		 0 Verified all 6 ticket premises in 38s, passed 2 Critic rounds, and automatically re-ran a flaky cloud CI job (gh run rerun --failed) to green. 0
5. TICKET-227: The Double Context Lobotomy
(Tests whether a 351-step math/binary ticket falls apart when the 200k window resets mid-commit) 		351 steps
5 subagents		 2 (233k & 46k) Hit auto-compaction 1 second after I said "ok to commit and push". Woke up, read 00_governance.md..99_next_action.md, and finished 45/45 tests with 0 reminders. 0

Let's walk through how these five tickets, the mid-flight Claude-to-Gemini swap, and the GPT-OSS 120B crash test played out in the transcripts.

3. Finding #1: Beating the +30% Code-Bloat Trap Before Writing a Single Line of Code (TICKET-553, TICKET-779, TICKET-482)

Why did the 718 companies in the Harvard study end up with +30% more code and 0% more finished tickets?

Because in a real engineering backlog, tickets rot. Between the day somebody files a ticket and the day an engineer picks it up, other PRs merge, architecture decisions change, and half the work often gets solved somewhere else.

Hand a normal AI agent a stale ticket, and its "Yes-Man" training (Part 3.9) forces it to say "Certainly!" and write the code anyway:

  • On TICKET-779, the ticket asked to add set -euo pipefail guards to our .scripts/*.sh files and enforce a 32 KB size limit on AGENTS.md. Before writing a plan, my Target 15 Archaeologist checked the repo, proved the .sh scripts already had set -euo pipefail on main, and cut the job in half.
  • On TICKET-482, the ticket listed 19 creation dialogs that needed error-banner handling. The Archaeologist inspected all 19 up front, proved 4 of them were already fixed on main, and scoped the plan strictly to the remaining 15.

And then there was TICKET-553—the poster child for the Harvard study's +30% code bloat.

TICKET-553 was a High priority ticket asking the developer to build a pre-signout wrapper (PreSignOutFirebaseAuth) that deletes the user's push-notification token from the database before calling FirebaseAuth.instance.signOut().

If you only look at today's files on HEAD, that wrapper isn't there—so a standard AI agent would happily crank out ~280 lines of code across 4 files and open a pull request.

Instead, my Target 15 Codebase Archaeologist ran git log -p across recent history (SCAR-ARCH-20) and wrote down a devastating finding in 15_archaeology_receipt.md:

  • Two weeks after TICKET-553 was filed, a developer working on a sibling ticket in PR #927 had already written that exact 243-line PreSignOutFirebaseAuth wrapper!
  • During code review on PR #927, our human lead architect explicitly rejected the wrapper, explaining that wrapping FirebaseAuth is brittle across SDK upgrades and unnecessary because post-signout cleanup + server-side pruning already handles stale tokens. A follow-up commit deleted the wrapper before PR #927 merged—leaving the older duplicate TICKET-553 sitting forgotten in the backlog like an unexploded bomb!

Because our workflow stamps any ticket claim that collides with codebase history as CONTRADICTED, the agent was forbidden to promise code. Instead, it came back to me with a Counter-Offer:

  • Plan A (Recommended — 0 files, 0 lines of code): Accept the Archaeologist's receipt, skip coding, post the PR #927 history onto TICKET-553, and close the ticket.
  • Plan B (4 files, ~280 lines of code): Overrule the lead architect and build the rejected wrapper anyway.

My entire review took four seconds: "plan A is fine. If he has already spoken, I'm not challenging."

Even better, because our workflow is a 1976 Makefile rather than a rigid 21-step checklist, an approved plan with zero target files didn't require any GOTO spaghetti: Target 30 (code), Target 40 (critic), Target 50 (commit), Target 60 (push), and Target 70 (PR checks) all reported Up to date (Nothing to be done) automatically, jumping straight to Target 80 to document and close the issue in 8 minutes, 29 seconds.

4. Finding #2: Beating the +49% Review Bottleneck with Pre-Commit Critics and One-Shot Bot Triage (TICKET-482)

What happens when a ticket does require changing 15 files across four packages?

In the Harvard study, developers push the AI's first green test straight to GitHub, where human reviewers wait 3.45 days only to bounce the PR back (2x bounce rate) or drown in +35% more bot comments.

In TICKET-482 (PR #1234), we saw how the Commitment Machine stops both problems before a human ever opens the PR:

A. Catching a Sneaky Flutter Linter Blind Spot (SCAR-RIV-14)

While updating the 15 creation dialogs so failed saves keep the modal open and display an error banner, the agent wrote the textbook Flutter pattern to satisfy the use_build_context_synchronously lint—capturing ScaffoldMessenger.of(context) and AppLocalizations.of(context) before the await line:

// Captured before the await so use_build_context_synchronously is happy:
final messenger = ScaffoldMessenger.of(context);
final local = AppLocalizations.of(context);

final result = await notifier.create(...);
isLoading.value = false;

// ⚠️ THE LINTER BLIND SPOT (SCAR-RIV-14):
notifier.onCreated(result, messenger, local);
if (!result.hasError && result.hasValue && context.mounted) {
  Navigator.of(context).pop(result.value);
}

Because the word context doesn't appear inside notifier.onCreated(result, messenger, local), flutter analyze --fatal-infos passed with 0 warnings!

Yet if the user closes the modal while await notifier.create(...) is waiting on the network, messenger (which belongs to the parent screen behind the dialog) is still alive—so notifier.onCreated(...) pops up a ghost SnackBar on the parent screen after the modal is already gone!

Instead of a senior engineer having to catch that subtle bug on GitHub three days later:

  1. Our automated review triage (Target 70) flagged the unguarded post-await call.
  2. The TDD Implementation Engineer wrote a Completer<void> widget test that closed the dialog mid-flight and proved the ghost SnackBar bug failed (red_exit = 1).
  3. It wrapped notifier.onCreated, any post-await ref.read(...), and Navigator.pop inside a single outer if (context.mounted) { ... } block (green_exit = 0), and a fresh Round 2 Model: "pro" Adversarial Critic (40_critic_review.md) verified all 14 dialogs before asking me to land.
  4. At Target 90, that trap was permanently recorded as SCAR-RIV-14 so no future agent gets fooled by pre-await ScaffoldMessenger handles.

B. One-Comment Bot Triage & The Mermaid Cockpit (SCAR-PROC-127)

When the GitHub review bot flagged that context.mounted pattern across 14 dialog files (C-1..C-14), our old rules would have burned 28 separate API calls (14 REST +1 reactions + 14 GraphQL resolveReviewThread calls) just closing threads one by one.

At Step 330, I made a simple observation: "generally, we just post one final PR comment instead of closing threads... Yeah, per-thread resolution burns a lot of redundant tokens." That became SCAR-PROC-127: the agent posts one consolidated PR triage table (gh pr comment <PR> --body-file <scratch>/triage_comment.md), paired with our 2-Push Bot Circuit Breaker (SCAR-REVIEW-27) so the agent never gets stuck in an endless ping-pong loop over minor Round 2 bot nitpicks.

And because 99_next_action.md renders a live color-coded Mermaid Commitment Diagram (:::done green, :::active blue, :::gate gold) right in my IDE sidebar, I don't even open the GitHub PR page anymore—I just wait for the green board.

5. Finding #3: /etc/init.d Files Make Your Agent Both Lobotomy-Proof (TICKET-227) and Vendor-Agnostic (Claude -> Gemini at Step 433)

The third reason long AI coding sessions fail in production is that the model either runs out of context tokens (200k lobotomy) or runs out of provider quota halfway through a big ticket.

Because our workflow keeps all commitment state in numbered Unix files on disk (<brain>/state/00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md) and forces subagents (fork()) to do the heavy reading and testing in their own throwaway windows (SCAR-PROC-95), we survived two extreme stress tests:

  1. Surviving Two Context Resets (TICKET-227): On TICKET-227 (351 steps, 45 unit tests), the IDE hit its context limit and triggered auto-compaction (CHECKPOINT) at Step 188 (233,658 -> 43,077 tokens)—literally 1 second after I typed "ok to commit and push"—and then hit a second reset at Step 350. In a normal chat session, getting lobotomized right after "ok to commit and push" is fatal: the model forgets whether the Critic ran or what it was about to commit. With Target 00: read-init-d, the agent woke up on Step 189, read 00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md off the disk, and picked up on the very next tool call with 0 nudges.
  2. Swapping Claude Sonnet 4.6 for Gemini 4 in Mid-Air (Step 433 of 960): During a marathon 960-step UI verification run on PR #1234 (FT-184, booting local emulators and driving an iOS Simulator to capture 5 live screenshots), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Thinking) hit its provider quota wall and died at Step 432. Instead of starting over, I clicked the IDE model picker, switched from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Gemini 4, and typed "continue". At Step 434, Gemini 4 read the /etc/init.d files Claude had written to disk, saw the exact target state, fixed the Xcode 26 simulator window issue in 20 steps, captured all 5 iOS screenshots, and finished the run!

When your workflow state lives in plain text files on disk instead of inside one vendor's context window, the LLM is just a swappable CPU running against a persistent hard drive.

6. Finding #4: The Capability Floor—Why GPT-OSS 120B Crashed and Burned in the Same Cockpit (791 Steps)

That mid-flight swap from Claude to Gemini begged the obvious question:

If the smarts live in the external Makefile and /etc/init.d files on disk, how small or cheap a model can wear the suit? Can you drop an open-weight 120B model into the exact same cockpit and get a senior engineer for free?

To find out, I took TICKET-894 ("Harden entity fromJson deserialization for legacy creator keys, timestamps, and nested maps"—the follow-up ticket split out of TICKET-482) and ran an A/B test in the exact same IDE with the exact same rules and tools: first with open-weight GPT-OSS 120B (Medium) for 791 steps (67 minutes) until I pulled the plug, and then with Gemini 4 (FT-222), which finished the ticket cleanly with 0 nudges.

Here is the scorecard from that 791-step crash test:

What Happened on TICKET-894 Frontier Model (Gemini 4) Open-Weight Test (GPT-OSS 120B) Why GPT-OSS 120B Failed
/etc/init.d State Files (<brain>/state/*.md) 100% (00..99 written) 0 files created Ignored SKILL.md and Turn-1 rules completely.
fork() Subagents Spawned (SCAR-PROC-95) 100% (Archaeologist, TDD, Critic) 0 subagents forked Dumped all 104 shell commands and 52 file reads into the main window.
Context Lobotomies (CHECKPOINT) 0 6 compactions (Steps 119..772) Flooded its own window, then woke up with total amnesia 6 times.
Botched Tool Calls (ERROR_MESSAGE) 0 (0.0%) 50 errors (13.6% of turns) Printed raw JSON tool syntax inside its <thinking> block with empty output.
Searching Google for Private Local Code 0 13 calls (search_web) Used Google Web Search to look for private Dart classes inside our own repo!
Simultaneous Background git commit Jobs 1 (waited cleanly) 6 running at once Set WaitMsBeforeAsync: 0 on git commit, then ran rm -f .git/index.lock while commits were still alive!
Outcome Merged (0 nudges) Aborted at Step 791 (18 nudges) Failed to finish any of the 4 ticket items.

Two scenes from GPT-OSS 120B's flight recorder tell the whole story:

  • Finding ParseLegacy, Getting Lobotomized, and Searching Google for It (Steps 90–213): At Step 91 (after I nudged it to stop searching Google and run rg locally), GPT-OSS 120B found ParseLegacy in packages/helpers/lib/src/json/json.dart and noted in its thoughts that ParseLegacy already handled int and map. Because it never wrote 15_archaeology_receipt.md to disk, Compaction #1 hit at Step 119 and wiped that file path from its memory. Waking up with no /etc/init.d files on disk, GPT-OSS 120B called Google Web Search (search_web(query: "ParseLegacy")) twice (Steps 192 & 196), announced "I'm still not seeing the ParseLegacy implementation in this repository", and spent the next 580 steps inventing a brand-new duplicate ParseLegacyAuth class from scratch!
  • Zero-Millisecond git commit Fork-Bombing (Steps 480–710): On 7 of its 10 git commit calls, GPT-OSS 120B passed WaitMsBeforeAsync: 0—backgrounding git commit #1 after 0 milliseconds while it still held .git/index.lock. On the next turn, it fired git commit #2, hit Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists, ran rm -f .git/index.lock while git commit #1 was still running, and launched five more background git commit jobs all corrupting the same Git index at once!

The Four "Driver's License" Checks for Any Autonomous Model

Why can Gemini 4 (Low) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 cruise through the Makefile workflow with zero repeat regressions, while GPT-OSS 120B drove straight into a ditch?

Because an external checklist and dashboard can replace deep puzzle-solving (Low vs. High thinking), but they cannot help a driver who can't read the steering wheel. Before any model can use a Makefile and /etc/init.d harness, it must pass four basic "driver's license" checks:

  1. Turn-1 Rule Obedience: Does it actually open SKILL.md and create 00_governance.md on Turn 1 before editing code?
  2. Clean Tool Calling: Can it invoke tools cleanly without dumping raw JSON inside its <thinking> thoughts?
  3. Basic Tool Sense: Does it know to search local files with rg instead of Google Web Search, and to wait for git commit instead of backgrounding it after 0ms?
  4. Honest Error Reporting: When a tool returns ERROR, does it report the failure honestly instead of hallucinating "I've posted the plan to Linear!"?

7. Summary: What the Commitment Machine Delivers—And What Comes Next

When you put the Harvard study's 718-company bottleneck next to these 2,677 steps of live production telemetry (926 steps across 5 tickets + 960 steps on FT-184 + 791 steps on GPT-OSS 120B), the takeaway is crystal clear:

  • Don't optimize for typing speed (+30% LOC); optimize for pre-commit truth (Counter-Offers + Local Critics). Making it legal—and mandatory—for an Archaeologist subagent to stamp a bad ticket CONTRADICTED (TICKET-553) and for a local Adversarial Critic to catch subtle framework bugs (TICKET-482) before git commit is how you keep junk out of your human reviewers' queues.
  • Put your agent's brain on the filesystem (/etc/init.d), not in the context window. Plain numbered Markdown files on disk turn 200k-token context resets and mid-flight vendor quota walls (Claude Sonnet 4.6 -> Gemini 4 at Step 433) into minor speed bumps.
  • Respect the model capability floor. Give the Makefile suit to a frontier model (Gemini 4 or Claude Sonnet 4.6) that passes the four Driver's License checks—and save the sub-threshold local models for Part 9, where we'll train those exact four reflexes directly into the weights via LoRA / DPO.

Next Up in Part 3.12: "Is This a Step, or Is This a Sensor?"

Right after I published Part 3.10, systems programmers, security researchers, compiler writers, and even an autonomous AI agent running on Claude Opus 5.5 started red-teaming the Commitment Machine in the comments—asking:

  • "The Makefile stops a check from being skipped—but what stops the agent from faking the green light when it controls the test file too?" (Sam LABBE & howcani howcani)
  • "Once RETRACTED is a legal move, what stops a lazy agent from claiming a method doesn't exist just to bail out of a hard ticket?" (Dawn / Sentient_Dawn)
  • "Why do prompt files rewritten by LLMs bloat by +145.8% and turn sharp numbers into mush—and how do you scale past 500 Scars without blowing up your context window?" (Vinnie Falco, Ctbhatia, & Subhadeep Chatterjee)

In Part 3.12, we'll look at how their feedback upgraded our workflow with read-only test pins, Linux insmod Loadable Scar Modules, and package:synthetic_scars_lint—turning prompt scars into 15ms compiler auto-fixes that cost zero prompt tokens and zero LLM retry turns.

articles.title: 6 Ways AI Changes OSINT (For People Who Already Do It Manually)
articles.description: You were pivoting before it was a prompt. Here's what the machines actually add to the craft — and...
articles.body_html:
You were pivoting before it was a prompt. Here's what the machines actually add to the craft — and what they still can't do for you.

There are two kinds of people reading this. The ones who discovered OSINT last year because an AI told them it was a lucrative career path, and the ones who were manually pivoting through breach dumps, certificate logs, and decade-old forum posts while the rest of the world was still asking chatbots to write haikus about the weather.

This one's for group two.

You don't need the craft explained to you, and you can smell a thought-leader post from three tabs away. So no hype here, no "AI will replace investigators," no carousel energy. Just six changes that are actually real, rated honestly by someone who respects your workflow: some of these will save you hours, one of them will save your case, and all of them come with fine print the demos never mention.

1. Local models killed the "where can I safely paste this" problem

Every investigator knows the reflex. You're holding a juicy chunk of text — a scraped bio, a membership list, sixty pages of forum rambling from a guy who definitely did the thing — and before you run it through a cloud tool, you pause. Whose servers does this touch? Whose logs does it land in? Am I about to leak my case to a third party to save twenty minutes?

Local models ended that negotiation. Run an open-weights model on your own hardware — Ollama, LM Studio, whatever fits your stack — and the entire analysis loop closes on your machine. Entity extraction, timeline reconstruction, matching three different transliterations of the same alias: all offline, all private, all yours.

This isn't a nice-to-have. If your work touches journalists' sources, confidential clients, or anything with a legal tail, "I uploaded the dossier to a chatbot" is not a sentence you want to say out loud in any room with better acoustics than a parking garage.

And the hardware bar is lower than the pitch decks claim. A mid-range machine runs 7B to 14B parameter models comfortably, and for extraction-grade tasks that's plenty. You don't need a data center. You need discipline.

2. Summarization got free. Judgment didn't.

AI is genuinely, almost offensively good at one thing OSINT people hate: reading garbage. Four hundred pages of scraped soup. Eleven thousand forum posts. A company's entire changelog since 2014. A model compresses that into structure in minutes, for free, without complaint.

But compression is not investigation. The model will faithfully summarize everything — except the one detail that mattered, because it doesn't know what mattered. It has no case. No stake. No memory of the alias that felt wrong on Tuesday.

So the division of labor is simple: the machine reads the corpus, you decide the next hop. The moment you offload the "what's next" decision too, you get the average of everything. And the average of everything is exactly where investigations go to die.

Pivot logic is still the product. You've just been promoted off the reading engine.

3. Prompt pipelines turn one-off queries into repeatable tradecraft

If your entire AI technique is retyping "extract all usernames, emails, phone numbers and organizations from this text" every session, you're using a language model like a vending machine. It works. It's also the tradecraft equivalent of re-typing your wordlists by hand each time.

The practitioners actually getting leverage build prompt libraries the way they built bash aliases: written once, tested against known input, versioned, reused. Same input schema in, same output schema out. Which means results become diffable — you can run the same extraction prompt across thirty groups, or across the same source today versus last month, and compare structure instead of squinting at vibes.

That's the difference between doing OSINT and owning an OSINT workflow. Your prompts are tradecraft. Write them like it: store them with your tooling, review them like code, and stop keeping your best one in a chat history you'll never find again.

4. Agents are sentries, not oracles

The real unlock isn't asking an AI questions. It's having something that watches while you don't.

Agent-assisted correlation looks like this: scheduled runs that check whether your target's username just appeared on a platform you haven't covered. Monitors that watch domains adjacent to your subject for content changes. A quiet loop over paste sites and fresh breach drops, matching against your indicators, pinging you only when an edge in the graph actually moves.

You stop losing whole afternoons to "did anything change since Tuesday?" The machine watches the graph. You get pinged when it matters.

This is also where your case notes stop being a graveyard and become infrastructure. If your research lives in a connected structure — an Obsidian vault, a graph tool, whatever you actually maintain — an agent can walk it, re-check stale nodes, and surface the dead-end lead from 2021 that just got interesting again.

One rule, learned expensively by the field: an agent that acts without logged reasoning is a liability with a nicer interface. Make it show its work.

5. Cross-language pivots got cheap

Non-English sources used to be a wall. Behind it: entire regional platforms, marketplaces, and forums that knew they were invisible to the average investigator — and behaved accordingly. Either you spoke the language, you paid a translator, or you had a very high tolerance for machine translation's avant-garde poetry.

Multimodal models kicked that wall down. They read the signage in the corner of a photo. They translate regional slang without collapsing. They notice that the storefront in the background, the vegetation, and the watermark style on a classified listing all point the same direction. The uncaptioned photo your target posted now says: this is a Portuguese-speaking area, and this watermark pattern is common to Brazilian listing sites.

Verification stays yours — models hallucinate place names with unshakeable confidence, and confident is not correct. But the wall became a door. And if you only ever hunted in English, understand that your hit rate was artificially capped your whole career. Most of the internet is not in English. Your targets, as it turns out, knew that.

6. Your targets have AI too

The uncomfortable one. The same tooling that accelerates you accelerates everyone you investigate.

Synthetic personas now ship with generated faces, coherent five-year posting histories, and opinions that poll well. Sockpuppets are written by language models and no longer smell like 2019-era bots. Voice cloning turns "urgent call from the client" into a convincing thirty seconds.

So provenance is the new baseline, not a bonus round. Account age versus content depth. The too-coherent biography. The contact who can only ever communicate in text. Verify through a second channel before you trust a first impression — every single time.

Here's the craft correction the panic posts miss: AI didn't kill OSINT. It killed lazy OSINT. Verification went from "best practice" to "the entire job," and honestly? That's a promotion for the people who were doing it right anyway.

And the paranoid cherry on top: some of what you scrape is now AI-generated noise, seeded specifically to poison collectors. Telling signal from slop is a billable skill now.

What AI still can't do

A credibility check, because someone always needs one.

The model doesn't know which lead stinks. It can't feel the wrongness of an alibi that's technically plausible but rhythmically off. It doesn't get warrants, doesn't testify, doesn't carry the ethics of the craft, and will never once wonder whether it should.

Feed it garbage and it returns confident, beautifully formatted garbage — the most dangerous file format in existence. It will connect two entities that share nothing but a typo and present the connection with the calm authority of a court exhibit.

Judgment, gut feel, documentation discipline, ethics: still yours. The machine raises your ceiling. It does not lower your standards. An AI-native investigator with manual-era fundamentals is a genuine nightmare for the other side. The reverse is a chat bubble with a subscription.

Start small, start loud

Three moves this week, none of which require cosplaying:

One: run a local model. Ollama and a 7B-class model on hardware you already own. First rule of the AI-native vault: nothing about a case leaves your machine.

Two: build five reusable prompts. Extraction, summarization, timeline, contradiction-checking, username-mapping. Version them, test them, keep them next to your wordlists.

Three: wire the outputs into your graph. If your notes don't compound, you're still reset-every-session — which is precisely the manual-era problem this whole wave was supposed to fix.

The ghost route taught you that privacy is a practice, not a purchase. Same energy here: the toolkit changes, the operator remains.

articles.title: 98 Calls, 98 Errors, 0 Detections: The Bug My Test Suite Called Green
articles.description: A detector returned None on every call for two full corpus runs, and the test suite reported green...
articles.body_html:
A detector returned None on every call for two full corpus runs, and the test suite reported green the whole time.

Not "it ran and found nothing." It never executed a successful call. Every signal I trusted — green tests, firing detectors, clean telemetry — said fine. The only reason I found it is one line in a summary file I'd been skimming past.

This is the kind of bug except Exception: return None makes possible, and most of us have written that line.

The run that looked great

I was piloting 100 synthetic agent traces through the LLM-augmented detectors in agentwatch — one tool in agentic-suite, a suite of open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI agents. The summary came back and it looked genuinely good:

traces_processed: 100
chat_calls: 363
embed_calls: 98
errors: 98
total_tokens: 52,578
json_parse_success: 363
json_parse_fail: 0

363 chat calls. 100% JSON parse success. 52,578 tokens. Detectors firing: hallucination: 98, confusion_pattern: 2, quality_degradation: 1. All sensible numbers.

Then one line: embed_calls: 98, errors: 98.

Every single embedding call failed. And I didn't notice — because the corpus run counts fires, not non-fires. A detector that never fires doesn't show up as "0." It's simply absent. And absent is not zero. Absent means this detector never ran.

This wasn't the first time, either. An earlier run, FT-11b, had 24 embed calls with 24 errors — same 100% failure rate, same invisibility. The bug had been there across two full corpus runs (FT-11b at 25 traces, FT-11d at 100 traces), and between them 122 embed calls had all failed. The error rate was in the telemetry the whole time; it just wasn't in the assertions.

The error was sitting in the logs the entire time:

LLM embed call failed: Error code: 404 - {'error': {'message':
"Model 'all-MiniLM-L6-v2' not found. Available models:
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-4bit, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit, Qwen3-8B-4bit,
Qwen3.5-4B-4bit, Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit"}}}

Logged 98 times. The tests passed, so nobody went looking for it.

The code path that made it invisible

The client was written to be resilient — a failed embedding shouldn't crash the pipeline:

async def embed(self, text):
    try:
        resp = await client.embeddings.create(model=self.embed_model, input=text)
        return list(resp.data[0].embedding)
    except Exception as exc:
        self._record_error(start)
        logger.warning("LLM embed call failed: %s", exc)
        return None  # ← silent failure

The detector treats None as "no vector available," which is reasonable:

current_vector = await self._client.embed(output_text)
if current_vector is None:
    return None  # "can't compare vectors → no anomaly"

And the test reads None as "didn't fire," which is correct for a negative case:

fired = anomaly is not None
fire_ok = fired == scenario.expect_fire   # False == False → pass

Three different meanings collapsed into one None:

A None from "I checked and found no anomaly" == a None from "I couldn't check because the API failed" == a None from "I never called the API at all."

Without call telemetry, those are indistinguishable. All three look like a passing negative case.

The reason this stayed hidden in the corpus runs is structural. Those runs count fires. output_drift wasn't "0" in the anomaly counts — it was absent. And absent reads exactly like "the detector ran and found nothing" when you're scanning a summary.

Making the detector actually work

The endpoint had no embedding model at all. OMLX only serves chat completions — all-MiniLM-L6-v2 isn't on the list. So when embed() comes back empty, I now ask the same model to rate how similar two texts are, on a 0-to-1 scale:

if current_vector is not None and baseline is not None:
    sim = cosine_similarity(current_vector, baseline)
else:
    # Embedding unavailable — fall back to chat-based similarity
    sim = await self._chat_similarity(baseline_text, output_text)
distance = 1.0 - sim
if distance >= self._threshold:
    return Anomaly(..., evidence={"method": "chat-fallback", ...})

The prompt is small and strict: "Compare two texts and rate their semantic similarity on a scale of 0.0 to 1.0. Return only JSON: {"similarity": <float>}." The distance is 1.0 - similarity. It's coarser than vector cosine — the model gives you a judgment, not a continuous metric — but it gets the fire-or-don't-fire decision right.

tip: When a primary API is unavailable, a chat-based fallback can produce correct verdicts with the same model. The tradeoff is precision, not correctness. Record the method in the evidence dict so operators know which path produced a given verdict.

There's a subtlety I almost missed. The first call has to set the baseline, so it returns None regardless — same as the vector path. The fallback only kicks in on the second call forward, once there's a baseline text to compare against. Get that ordering wrong and you fire on the very first trace, which is noise.

The check I should have written first

This is the part most suites skip. Before each scenario, snapshot the client's call counters. After, measure the delta for that scenario:

stats_before = dict(client._stats)
anomaly = await det.detect_async(summary, spans, pool=None)
stats_after = dict(client._stats)

llm_calls = stats_after["chat_calls"] - stats_before["chat_calls"]
embed_calls = stats_after["embed_calls"] - stats_before["embed_calls"]
llm_called_ok = (llm_calls + embed_calls) > 0

ok = fire_ok and sev_ok and type_ok and expl_ok and evid_ok and llm_called_ok

If the LLM was never called, the scenario fails — even if the detector returned the "right" answer. A silent None with zero calls is a hidden skip, not a pass.

That check is the difference between a real pass and a hidden skip, and it's the one most suites don't have. It's also cheap: the client already tracks its own call counts for telemetry, so the harness just reads them.

After the fix, both scenarios run with real calls and real evidence:

✅ ED1  output_drift  fire=True   sev=critical  llm_calls=1  llm_errors=2
✅ ED2  output_drift  fire=False  sev=None      llm_calls=1  llm_errors=2

The two llm_errors are the failed embed calls — still 404, still logged, but now they don't define the outcome. The one llm_calls is the chat fallback doing the actual work. The model's actual verdicts:

ED1 (completely different texts):  {"similarity": 0.1}   → distance 0.9 → fires critical
ED2 (nearly identical texts):      {"similarity": 0.95}  → distance 0.05 → silent (correct)

Both were the right call. And this time I can prove the model actually made them.

This isn't about embeddings

The shape repeats anywhere a dependency returns a sentinel on failure:

Dependency Sentinel Looks like
LLM embed() None "no anomaly"
DB fetchrow() None "no baseline"
HTTP GET "" "no data"
Cache get() None "not in cache"
File read() "" "file is empty"

In every case, the failure wears the costume of legitimate emptiness. The test passes. The system is broken. Nobody knows — until someone counts the calls or checks the status, which is the thing the test didn't do.

The fix is always the same shape: prove the dependency was exercised, not just check the output. Count the calls. Check the response status. Assert the network was reached. A None return is only trustworthy if you can prove the call happened.

What I changed

A missing anomaly type is not "zero anomalies." It's "this detector never ran." Check for presence, not just count.

Log warnings are not alerts. The 404 was logged 98 times in one run, 24 in an earlier one, and nobody saw it. If a failure matters, make it an assertion, not a log line.

None is a terrible sentinel because it doesn't tell you which of its three meanings it has. "I checked," "I couldn't check," and "I never tried" all collapse into the same value and the same passing test.

The deeper habit change for me was the assertion. Before this, my tests asked "did the detector return the right answer?" After this, they also ask "did it actually do the work that produces an answer?" The first question can be satisfied by accident. The second one can't.

All of it is fixed in agentwatch v0.1.0, with the llm_called_ok check enforced on every LLM scenario.

The question worth asking of your own repo: which green test would still pass if the service behind it were down? The answer is usually the one that asserts the output but never asserts the dependency ran.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (defect D-4)
  • Raw LLM I/O: llm-scenario-io.jsonl
  • Harness: scenario_validation.py

articles.title: Most Package Managers Won't Stop a Tampered Download by Default
articles.description: Trail of Bits tested 25 package managers against a compromised server. Only Go and vcpkg verified every download. Here's what to change in your CI.
articles.body_html:
Keegan Ryan of the security firm Trail of Bits set up a fake compromised package server and pointed 25 popular package managers at it. Two of them, Go and vcpkg, verified every package they downloaded, even without a lockfile. Without one, the other 23 installed whatever they were given.

Lockfiles didn't rescue most of them either.

The test

Ryan routed each tool's traffic through a proxy that could rewrite downloads, then installed quickstart projects with default settings, with and without a lockfile. An attack counted as a success if the injected code ran. The threat model assumes any web-facing server, such as a registry or a mirror, can be compromised, but backend secrets like private signing keys can't.

The lockfile is the safety net, and it's mostly unplugged

A lockfile pins every dependency's exact version and, ideally, a hash: a fingerprint the download has to match. Fewer than half of the 25 tools checked those hashes by default.

All 25 package managers, by default behavior. Source: Trail of Bits, October 14, 2026.

Nine verify when a lockfile is present, including npm, pnpm, Cargo, uv and Yarn. Five can verify, but only with extra steps. The last nine don't verify lockfile hashes at all, or the check doesn't apply to them.

Checks that don't stop anything

Tools with no check are the obvious failures. The sneakier ones run a check and install anyway:

  • Pub (Dart and Flutter) detects a hash mismatch, installs the package anyway and updates the lockfile to match, unless you pass --enforce-lockfile. Some Flutter commands run pub get too, and can overwrite the lockfile unless called with --no-pub.
  • pnpm overwrote the lockfile on a mismatch until version 11.4, in May 2026, so the tampered package simply became the new truth.
  • Composer (PHP) locks a Git commit, then downloads a ZIP archive it never checks against that commit.
  • CocoaPods hashes the package spec but fetches the source by Git tag, which a compromised host could serve with different contents.
  • cpanminus (Perl) still connects to its repository over plain HTTP by default.

Four outcomes when the download and the lockfile disagree. Only the green one protects you.

Why the defaults are like this

None of this is hidden; it's documented behavior. Lockfiles were built for reproducible installs, and as Ryan notes, reading them through a supply-chain lens "is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design." Strict pinning also has a cost: every update, security fixes included, needs a lockfile change.

Go shows the alternative. It checks every hash against a signed checksum database that works like a transparency log, which makes targeted tampering much harder, at the cost of concentrating trust in a single private key. It was the only tool that verified every download and checked signatures by default. As Ryan puts it, "Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago."

What to do this week

  1. Commit your lockfile, at least for applications. Norms for libraries vary by ecosystem.
  2. Install in strict mode in CI: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, uv sync --locked, pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt (with hashes generated by pip-compile --generate-hashes) or dart pub get --enforce-lockfile.
  3. If your tool needs extra steps, take them: the conda-lock library for Conda, a verification-metadata.xml file for Gradle, the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property for NuGet.
  4. If your tool is in the last group, don't treat its lockfile as a security control. Maven can check signatures against trusted keys with the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin. Beyond that, the fallback Conan's developers suggest applies widely: if integrity is critical, run your own repository server.

Then test it: change one hash in your lockfile on purpose and confirm CI fails.

Caveats

Each tool was tested with one package, one version and one platform, Ubuntu, and some setups, like PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu, don't reflect typical use. The study shows that reasonable defaults can leave you exposed, not that every setup is.

Verification comes before detection

Most supply chain tooling hunts for packages already known to be bad. This study is about the step before that: making sure the package you got is the package you asked for. For most of the 25 tools, that check is off by default or missing. Where it exists, turning it on is about the cheapest security win you'll find.

If you check what your package manager does on a hash mismatch, I'd like to hear what you find.

Sources

  • Package managers have an integrity problem, Keegan Ryan, Trail of Bits, October 14, 2026

articles.title: I Allocated 1.5 GB Just to Add Vectors Together
articles.description: C# 14 lets you write your own in-place +=. I used it to fold 200,000 vectors with zero allocations instead of 1.5 GB, and measured the gap.
articles.body_html:
I had a loop that did something embarrassingly simple: fold a stream of feature vectors into one running total. Add a vector, add the next, keep going. A few hundred thousand of them. The math is a for-loop over some doubles, nothing that should trouble the garbage collector.

The allocation profile said otherwise. Gigabytes. For adding numbers.

I knew why the second I looked at the operator. I'd written + the tidy, immutable way years ago and never thought about it again:

public static Vec operator +(Vec a, Vec b)
{
    var result = new double[a.Data.Length];
    for (int i = 0; i < result.Length; i++)
        result[i] = a.Data[i] + b.Data[i];
    return new Vec(result);
}

That's a perfectly reasonable operator. Every call hands back a brand new Vec with its own fresh array, nobody's state gets stomped, and you can reason about it without fear. It's also a fresh 8 KB array on the heap every single time you add two 1024-dimension vectors. In a one-off expression that's free. In a fold over a stream, it's a steady firehose into gen 0.

My accumulation loop was the firehose:

var acc = new Vec(Dims);
for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
    acc = acc + input[i];

Read that acc = acc + input[i] again. I'm allocating a whole new accumulator on every iteration and throwing the old one away. I never needed a new object. I wanted to pour the next vector into the one I already had.

The operator I couldn't write before

Until C# 14 there was no clean way to say that. += was always just sugar for a = a + b: it called your operator +, took the result, and assigned it back. You couldn't hook the "in place" part because there was no in-place part to hook.

C# 14 adds user-defined compound assignment operators. You write operator += as its own thing. It's an instance method, it returns void, and it mutates this.

public void operator +=(Vec other)
{
    var mine = Data;
    var theirs = other.Data;
    for (int i = 0; i < mine.Length; i++)
        mine[i] += theirs[i];
}

No new. No array. It reaches into the buffer this instance already owns and adds the other vector straight into it. The call site doesn't change at all: acc += input[i] now finds this operator instead of falling back to +. If I hadn't written it, the compiler would've quietly used operator + like always. You only get the new behavior when you opt in.

I counted it

I don't trust "should be faster," so I measured. I built 200,000 vectors of 1024 doubles each, folded them both ways, and tracked wall-clock time (best of five) alongside bytes allocated with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(). This is a container with workstation GC, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio and the allocation column, not the exact milliseconds.

dims=1024, vectors=200,000, rounds=5, GC=workstation

acc = acc + v   best    740.0 ms   allocated   1571.7 MB   checksum 102400896.09
acc += v        best    301.9 ms   allocated      0.0 MB   checksum 102400896.09

same result: True
time ratio:  2.45x

1.5 GB versus zero. Same checksum, so the two loops genuinely compute the same answer. The in-place version came out 2.45x faster, and most of that gap isn't the addition. It's the collector cleaning up a gigabyte and a half of short-lived arrays that never had any reason to exist. Zero megabytes still makes me grin a little. The whole fold runs without handing the GC a single byte.

When I'd leave the old operator alone

Here's the part the benchmark won't tell you: mutating in place throws away the one thing immutable + was buying you. With operator +, nobody's vector changes under them. With operator +=, if two references point at the same Vec and one of them does +=, the other just silently got mutated too. That's a classic aliasing bug, and it's exactly the kind of thing that's fine in a tight local loop and nasty in a shared domain model.

So I'm not about to replace every + with an in-place +=. For value-ish types you pass around, compare, and cache, immutability is worth more than the allocations. My honest rule: reach for the in-place operator when you've got a genuine hot accumulation loop and the accumulator is local and yours. Everywhere else, let + keep making new things.

One more sharp edge. The compiler doesn't enforce consistency, so you can define += without +, or make them disagree, and it won't say a word. I'd keep the two in sync regardless, because a += that quietly diverges from + is a debugging session waiting to happen.

I normally drop a link to the runnable sample here, but my code repo push got blocked this time, so the whole thing is right below. Target net10.0 with <LangVersion>14</LangVersion> and it runs as-is:

using System.Diagnostics;

sealed class Vec
{
    public readonly double[] Data;

    public Vec(int dims) => Data = new double[dims];
    public Vec(double[] data) => Data = data;

    // Immutable style: a fresh Vec + array on every add.
    public static Vec operator +(Vec a, Vec b)
    {
        var result = new double[a.Data.Length];
        for (int i = 0; i < result.Length; i++)
            result[i] = a.Data[i] + b.Data[i];
        return new Vec(result);
    }

    // C# 14 in-place compound assignment: mutates this buffer, allocates nothing.
    public void operator +=(Vec other)
    {
        var mine = Data;
        var theirs = other.Data;
        for (int i = 0; i < mine.Length; i++)
            mine[i] += theirs[i];
    }

    public double Checksum()
    {
        double s = 0;
        foreach (var d in Data) s += d;
        return s;
    }
}

static class Program
{
    const int Dims = 1024;
    const int Count = 200_000;
    const int Rounds = 5;

    static Vec[] BuildInputs()
    {
        var rng = new Random(42);
        var vecs = new Vec[Count];
        for (int i = 0; i < Count; i++)
        {
            var d = new double[Dims];
            for (int j = 0; j < Dims; j++) d[j] = rng.NextDouble();
            vecs[i] = new Vec(d);
        }
        return vecs;
    }

    static (double sum, long bytes, double ms) RunPlus(Vec[] input)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var acc = new Vec(Dims);
        for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
            acc = acc + input[i];
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Stop();
        return (acc.Checksum(), after - before, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }

    static (double sum, long bytes, double ms) RunCompound(Vec[] input)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var acc = new Vec(Dims);
        for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
            acc += input[i];
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Stop();
        return (acc.Checksum(), after - before, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"dims={Dims}, vectors={Count:N0}, rounds={Rounds}, GC=workstation");
        var input = BuildInputs();

        _ = RunPlus(input);      // warm up the JIT
        _ = RunCompound(input);

        double plusChk = 0, compChk = 0, plusBest = double.MaxValue, compBest = double.MaxValue;
        long plusBytes = 0, compBytes = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
        {
            var p = RunPlus(input);
            var c = RunCompound(input);
            plusChk = p.sum; compChk = c.sum;
            plusBytes = p.bytes; compBytes = c.bytes;
            if (p.ms < plusBest) plusBest = p.ms;
            if (c.ms < compBest) compBest = c.ms;
        }

        Console.WriteLine($"acc = acc + v   best {plusBest,8:F1} ms   allocated {plusBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),8:F1} MB   checksum {plusChk:F2}");
        Console.WriteLine($"acc += v        best {compBest,8:F1} ms   allocated {compBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),8:F1} MB   checksum {compChk:F2}");
        Console.WriteLine($"same result: {Math.Abs(plusChk - compChk) < 1e-6}");
        Console.WriteLine($"time ratio:  {plusBest / compBest:F2}x");
    }
}

Have you hit a spot where += was quietly allocating behind your back? I'd like to hear where it bit you.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: The string.Create I Didn't Need
articles.description: I set out to swap an interpolated cache key for string.Create to cut allocations. It allocated exactly the same. Here's what was actually wasting the memory.
articles.body_html:
A profiler started this one. I had a cache lookup on a hot path, and the key got built with string interpolation. During review someone suggested string.Create would allocate less. Reasonable. That's the standard advice when you're hunting garbage. So I went to make the swap, and out of habit I measured both before committing. They allocated exactly the same. Byte for byte. The thing I was "fixing" was already as lean as the fix.

The real lesson turned out to be somewhere I wasn't even looking.

The key, three ways

The key looks like user:42:profile:eu-west. An int in the middle, strings on either side. Here are the three ways I had on the table.

string NaiveConcat(int id, string region) =>
    "user:" + id + ":profile:" + region;

string Interpolated(int id, string region) =>
    $"user:{id}:profile:{region}";

string Created(int id, string region)
{
    int digits = id == 0 ? 1 : (int)Math.Floor(Math.Log10(Math.Abs(id))) + 1;
    if (id < 0) digits++;
    int len = 5 + digits + 9 + region.Length;   // "user:" + digits + ":profile:" + region
    return string.Create(len, (id, region), static (span, state) =>
    {
        var (i, r) = state;
        int pos = 0;
        "user:".CopyTo(span);              pos += 5;
        i.TryFormat(span[pos..], out int w); pos += w;
        ":profile:".CopyTo(span[pos..]);   pos += 9;
        r.CopyTo(span[pos..]);
    });
}

The first is how most of us write it without thinking. The second is how we write it once we've been told interpolation is fine. The third is what you reach for when you've decided allocations are the enemy and you want the floor.

Look how much more there is to that third one. I have to work out the exact length myself, digits and all. Get the math wrong and I either throw an ArgumentException or silently truncate the key, which in a cache is its own special kind of fun. That cost isn't in the benchmark. It's in the next person who has to read it.

I counted it

I didn't want to argue from vibes, so I built the smallest thing that would show the gap. Each method called five million times with an int and a region, allocations read with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the loop, best of seven rounds, a warmup pass and a full GC between rounds.

long Measure(Func<int, string, string> build)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) _ = build(i, "eu-west"); // warm up

    long best = long.MaxValue;
    for (int r = 0; r < 7; r++)
    {
        GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5_000_000; i++)
            sink += build(i, "eu-west").Length;   // sink keeps it from being elided
        best = Math.Min(best, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
    }
    return best;
}

The allocation counter is deterministic, so I trust it. Here's what came back:

naive  "+"           599,110,440 bytes    119.8 B/op       120 ms
interpolation        399,920,040 bytes     80.0 B/op       150 ms
string.Create        399,920,040 bytes     80.0 B/op       135 ms

What the numbers actually say

Two things jumped out.

First, interpolation and string.Create allocated the identical 80 bytes per call. Not close. Identical. The same 399,920,040 total, both runs. That 80 bytes is the finished string itself, and nobody gets to skip that one; you asked for a string, here's your string. The DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler the compiler builds for $"..." formats the int straight into a buffer and produces the result in a single allocation. string.Create does the same thing, except I'm the one filling the span by hand. The optimization I was about to commit bought me nothing on the metric I cared about.

Second, and this is the one that mattered: naive + allocated fifty percent more. 119.8 bytes against 80. When you write "user:" + id + ..., the int can't slot straight into a string, so it gets boxed and ToString'd into an extra little object that has nothing to do with the string you wanted. That was the drip in my profile. Not the interpolation I'd been told to replace. The plus signs I hadn't thought about at all.

I'll say the quiet part: string.Create is over-prescribed as an allocation fix. Most times I see it recommended, the thing it's replacing is plain interpolation, and for that it's a lateral move with worse readability.

A fair word on the timing, since someone always asks. string.Create did come in a bit quicker in wall clock, around 135ms against 150ms, at identical allocations. But that's a two-core container, best-of-seven, and I trust the byte counter a lot more than the stopwatch in here. If ten percent of throughput on this exact loop is the difference between shipping and not, go measure it on your box. It usually isn't.

When I'd actually reach for it

string.Create earns its keep when you're in a loop you've already profiled, the length is cheap to compute, and you've watched the throughput matter: formatting IDs, masking millions of card numbers in a tight path, that sort of thing. For a cache key you build a few thousand times a second, interpolation and move on with your life. Don't make the next reader parse length arithmetic to save zero bytes.

The change that's always worth making: stop gluing non-strings onto strings with +. Interpolate instead. Same readability, a third less garbage, and you never have to think about boxing again. That one's not a tradeoff, it's just free.

What's an optimization you cargo-culted for years before you ever measured it? I'd like to know I'm not the only one.

Still out here counting bytes nobody asked me to count.

articles.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell): Patch PHP Now
articles.description: TL;DR: On 21 October 2026, PHP released emergency updates for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619,...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: On 21 October 2026, PHP released emergency updates for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical vulnerabilities known together as PHP2Shell. Both are scored CVSS 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on any server handling web requests with PHP. Update to PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12, restart your workers, and verify the version your site actually serves. On PHP 8.1 or older there is no official patched release.

What are these vulnerabilities?

Both bugs live in the PHP engine itself, not in WordPress, Laravel, a plugin, or your code. The vulnerable code runs while PHP parses the request, before your application starts.

CVE-2026-109618 (RCE via OOM corruption). PHP bails out of a request when it runs out of memory. In some paths, request memory is reachable before it is fully initialized. If an allocation fails at that moment, the memory is left in an invalid state that later code can be tricked into trusting. There are several ways to drive PHP to that point during multipart body parsing while staying within configured limits. On Apache mod_php this happens before any application code runs.

CVE-2026-109619 (RCE via stale global state). PHP workers keep global state for errors, sessions, objects, and extensions. Some of that state points to memory owned by one request. After a bad request ending, leftover state can survive into the next request on the same worker and point at freed memory, a use-after-free that can end in code execution.

No authentication, no user interaction, and the attacker gets code execution with the web server account's permissions: config files, database credentials, web shells, the lot.

Who is affected?

Every PHP installation serving web requests: PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Mod_php is rated highest risk. On PHP-FPM, exploitation was confirmed for CVE-2026-109619 through session upload progress, and the CVE-2026-109618 code path is present.

The vulnerable patterns date back to PHP 5.4 era code, and exploitation attempts were observed days before the patch shipped. The technical details also leaked ahead of the planned disclosure.

Fixed versions

Released 21 October 2026:

  • PHP 8.2 → 8.2.35
  • PHP 8.3 → 8.3.36
  • PHP 8.4 → 8.4.27
  • PHP 8.5 → 8.5.12

Staying on your current branch is the fastest safe move. Distribution and LTS vendor packages may contain the fix under an older-looking version number, so check your vendor's security notice before trusting the version string alone.

Check the right PHP version

php -v tells you the CLI version. Your site may run a different PHP through PHP-FPM or mod_php. Temporarily drop this in your web root, load it, note the version, and delete the file immediately:

<?php phpinfo();

A phpinfo page left online hands attackers your paths and configuration. Also check staging sites, containers pinned to old image tags, and forgotten installs on the same server. Attackers scan for those first.

Patch steps

  1. Inventory every host, container, and hosting account running PHP, with its branch.
  2. Update PHP. On Docker, rebuild images on the patched tags and redeploy. On managed hosting, ask your provider to confirm in writing which patched build is running. Updating Composer dependencies does not fix this; it is a runtime update.
  3. Restart PHP-FPM and Apache. Running workers keep the old code until they restart.
  4. Verify the served version again through the web server.
  5. Smoke-test login, forms, and file uploads. The vulnerable paths sit inside multipart and session upload handling.

If you cannot update today

PHP's own position: there is no complete mitigation, and updating is the only safe option. These steps only reduce exposure to confirmed attack paths:

  • Set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 if you do not need upload progress tracking.
  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces = 0.
  • Block multipart uploads at the proxy or WAF on routes that do not need them, and restrict admin areas by IP or VPN.
  • If an internet-facing system cannot be patched or shielded, several national cyber agencies advised considering taking it offline.

Check whether you were already hit

Patching does not tell you whether someone got in first. Attempts were observed from at least 17 October. Review logs from that date for unusual multipart POSTs, session upload progress hits, abnormal content lengths, and bursts of 500 errors or worker crashes. Check upload and cache directories for recently modified PHP files, look for unknown files in the web root, and new admin accounts or cron jobs. If you find signs, treat it as an incident: preserve logs, rebuild clean, and rotate secrets.

The bigger lesson

Much of this incident's blast radius is servers running PHP versions that stopped receiving fixes years ago. They worked fine until they became the easiest targets on the internet. Keep runtimes inside their supported window, and keep an inventory of everywhere PHP runs.

Have you confirmed your patched version with your hosting provider yet, or are you still waiting?

articles.title: My Instagram tool's traffic was 82% Indonesian — so I taught it WhatsApp
articles.description: Search Console told me my Instagram chat analyzer's audience was mostly Indonesian — and WhatsApp-first — while the tool only spoke Instagram. This is the messy parsing work of fixing that.
articles.body_html:
The Search Console export that rewrote my roadmap

Stats Insta is a small tool I built for myself and then put online: upload an Instagram chat export, get statistics about your conversations — who texts most, when you're active, your top emojis, Wrapped-style story cards you can share. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

A few weeks ago I finally did the boring thing and exported sixteen months of Google Search Console data to actually look at it. Around 6,500 clicks. And 82% of them from Indonesia.

It gets stranger. Most of my top search queries weren't keywords at all — they were people typing my old Vercel domain name into Google to find their way back. Traffic had peaked back in December 2025 (Wrapped season, of course) and was slowly sliding. In other words: the tool had found an audience almost by accident, the audience was Indonesian, and it was loyal enough to Google a URL.

Here's the part that stung: Indonesia is a WhatsApp-first country. For most of my actual users, WhatsApp is not "an app" — it's the default layer for talking to everyone. And my tool supported exactly zero WhatsApp. Every one of those users was analyzing the chats they have on their secondary app, because the app they actually live in wasn't supported at all.

So the roadmap rewrote itself. Before any new features: teach the tool WhatsApp.

Two parsers, two completely different worlds

Instagram exports are a gift. You request your data, wait, and get message_1.json — real structured JSON with sender_name, timestamp_ms, a reactions array, the works. Parsing it is an afternoon.

A WhatsApp export is a .txt file that looks like a chat transcript, because it is one:

14/08/2025, 21:03 - Messages are end-to-end encrypted
14/08/2025, 21:04 - Priya: ok so about tomorrow
[14/08/2025, 21:04:37] Arjun: wait, which tomorrow?

That first line is Android format, the third is iOS. Neither is a standard — the comma is optional, seconds come and go, and the clock is 12-hour in some regions and 24-hour in others. The parser ended up starting with two regexes just to recognize a line:

const IOS_LINE =
  /^\[(\d{1,2})[./](\d{1,2})[./](\d{2,4}),?\s+(\d{1,2}):(\d{2})(?::(\d{2}))?\s*([AaPp]\.?[Mm]\.?)?\]\s?(.*)$/;
const ANDROID_LINE =
  /^(\d{1,2})[./](\d{1,2})[./](\d{2,4}),?\s+(\d{1,2}):(\d{2})(?::(\d{2}))?\s*([AaPp]\.?[Mm]\.?)?\s*[-\u2010-\u2015]\s+(.*)$/;

Then the real problems start:

Half the lines aren't messages. The encryption notice, "Priya added Arjun", subject changes, "security code changed", missed calls — all of it sits in the file wearing a timestamp, and all of it has to be excluded or your statistics count WhatsApp itself as a very talkative participant.

Some system lines disguise themselves as messages. Alice changed the subject to "Trip: Friday plans" contains a ": " — so a naive split happily parses it as a message from a person named "Alice changed the subject to "Trip". I ended up treating a "sender" as fake if it's implausibly long or contains a system verb before the colon.

Multi-line messages have no prefix at all. If someone sends a message with line breaks, the continuation lines arrive naked. The rule is simple — a line with no timestamp belongs to the previous message — but you only discover that after your message count doesn't match the chat you exported by hand.

The file is full of invisible characters. A BOM at the start, narrow no-break spaces before AM/PM, left-to-right marks wrapped around lines. Normalize them away first, or your regexes fail on files that look identical to the ones that work.

And the worst one: nobody tells you the date order. Is 03/04/2025 the 3rd of April or March 4th? WhatsApp doesn't label it, and guessing wrong swaps days and months across the entire history. The parser scans the whole file before parsing anything:

let dayFirst = true;
let sawMonthFirstEvidence = false;
for (const line of lines) {
  const raw = matchTimestampLine(line);
  if (!raw) continue;
  if (raw.first > 12) { dayFirst = true; break; } // 13+ can't be a month
  if (raw.second > 12) sawMonthFirstEvidence = true;
}
if (sawMonthFirstEvidence) dayFirst = false;

If any date's first number is above 12, it must be the day. If only the second number ever goes above 12, the file is month-first. If the file never gives unambiguous evidence — a short chat from the first twelve days of a month — it defaults to day-first, which matches the export locales of most of my users: Indonesia, India, Europe, Latin America. It's a heuristic, and I wrote it down as one in the code comments, because pretending it's a guarantee would be lying.

One stats engine, two front doors

The best decision in the whole project was refusing to build a second analyzer. The WhatsApp parser's only job is to normalize a messy text file into the exact same shape the Instagram path already produces:

{ [sender_name: string]: Message[] }

Because the model is identical, every existing statistic, chart and story card — totals, distribution, the activity heatmap, night owls, conversation starters — worked on WhatsApp chats the moment the parser did. Zero changes downstream.

The only additions were three optional flags on Message, and they turned out to be where the fun was:

  • isDeleted — "This message was deleted" arrives under the sender's name, so instead of discarding it, the parser keeps it as a flagged, content-less message. It counts toward that person's totals but is invisible to text statistics. That's what powers a Deleted Messages leaderboard — who in your group chat deletes the most.
  • isMedia — <Media omitted>, <attached: IMG-2041.jpg>, IMG-2041.jpg (file attached) (captions kept, when there are any). Powers Media Shared counts.
  • isEdited — WhatsApp appends <This message was edited> to edited messages, sometimes on its own line. The parser strips the marker and flags the message.

From those flags plus the plain text fell out a set of stats that make no sense for Instagram but are pure WhatsApp: Top Link Sharers, Questions Asked (who asks the most questions), Biggest Double-Texter, plus Signature Emoji, Fastest Responder (average reply gaps) and Morning Person. One graceful accident: WhatsApp exports carry no reaction data, so reaction-based stats simply find nothing — exactly what they already did for an Instagram chat where nobody reacted. Nothing needed special-casing.

What shipped

The tool now takes Instagram JSON and WhatsApp .txt/ZIP exports through the same upload box, tells them apart on its own, and runs the same engine on both. There's a dedicated WhatsApp page, WhatsApp-specific cards, a downloadable report, and Wrapped story cards that now say "WhatsApp" when they're about a WhatsApp chat (a detail I got wrong in the first version, and a user caught within hours — platform support means the copy, not just the parser).

Is it too early for a victory lap? Completely. The honest result so far is: the tool finally supports the app its audience actually uses. Whether the December slide reverses is a question the next Search Console export will answer, and I've learned my lesson about reading those more often.

If you want to try it — everything runs locally in your browser, your chats never leave your device:

  • The tool: https://stats-insta.vercel.app
  • WhatsApp chat analyzer: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/whatsapp-chat-analyzer
  • Guide — how to export a WhatsApp chat: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/guides/export-whatsapp-chat

And if you've ever parsed WhatsApp exports yourself and fought the date-order problem differently, I genuinely want to hear how. The comments are open.

articles.title: Give Your AI Feature a Kill Switch, a Budget, and a Paper Trail
articles.description: The second-most dangerous demo is "watch the agent do everything." The most dangerous is shipping...
articles.body_html:
The second-most dangerous demo is "watch the agent do everything." The most dangerous is shipping that demo to real users on Monday.

I build web and mobile products with Node, React, and Flutter, and I speak about AI in community spaces. The pattern I keep seeing: teams add a chat box or an "AI assistant" tab, wire an API key, and hope prompt vibes will behave in production. Hope is not an architecture.

This post is a practical starter kit for fullstack builders: three controls every AI feature should have before you invite non-technical users — a kill switch, a budget, and a paper trail. No cloud-vendor lock-in assumed. You can implement these with boring Node middleware and a small React admin panel.

Why demos lie

Figure: gate every model call — kill switch, budget, paper trail.

In a Meetup demo:

  • You are the only user
  • You type polite, on-distribution prompts
  • You ignore the bill
  • You can Ctrl+C when it loops
  • Nobody pastes a 40-page PDF of junk to "summarize"

In production:

  • Users paste secrets by accident
  • Prompts go adversarial or just confused
  • A retry storm turns into a surprise invoice
  • An agent tool call hits the wrong environment
  • You need to explain what happened three days later

Governance sounds enterprise. The core is simpler: assume the model will be wrong, expensive, or both — and design the blast radius.

Control 1: Kill switch (feature flags that actually stop spend)

A kill switch is not a blog toggle in Notion. It is a runtime gate checked before every model call and every tool invocation.

Minimal shape:

// lib/aiFlags.js
export async function assertAiEnabled(featureKey) {
  const row = await db.flags.get(featureKey);
  if (!row?.enabled) {
    const err = new Error("AI_FEATURE_DISABLED");
    err.code = "AI_FEATURE_DISABLED";
    throw err;
  }
}

Call it at the edge of your AI service:

export async function runAssistant({ userId, featureKey, input }) {
  await assertAiEnabled(featureKey);
  // ... budget check, then model call
}

Wire a React admin (or even a secured POST /admin/flags) so you can disable meetup-copilot without redeploying. When something smells wrong at 1 a.m., you want a button — not a pipeline.

Mobile note: Flutter clients should treat AI_FEATURE_DISABLED as a first-class UI state ("Assistant temporarily off"), not a generic 500. Users forgive maintenance; they do not forgive spinning forever.

Bonus: scoped kills

Prefer per-feature flags over a global "AI off":

  • chat.summarize
  • chat.reply-suggest
  • agent.tools.github (keep this off until you are truly ready)

That way a broken experimental agent does not take down a simple title-rewriter that still helps organizers.

Control 2: Budget (tokens, calls, and blast radius)

If you cannot answer "what is the max this feature can cost today?", you do not have a product — you have an open tab.

Soft limits per user / per org 

export async function assertWithinBudget({ tenantId, featureKey }) {
  const usage = await db.usage.today(tenantId, featureKey);
  const limit = await db.limits.get(tenantId, featureKey);

  if (usage.calls >= limit.maxCalls || usage.tokens >= limit.maxTokens) {
    const err = new Error("AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED");
    err.code = "AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED";
    throw err;
  }
}

Practical defaults for an early community product:

  • Cap calls per user per day
  • Cap max input characters (reject the 2MB paste early)
  • Cap max tool iterations for agents (e.g. 5 steps, then stop with a clear message)
  • Separate "playground" keys from "production" keys

Hard limits at the provider

Also set provider-side spending caps where they exist. Application budgets fail closed when Redis hiccups; provider caps fail closed when your app has a bug. Use both.

Agents need step budgets, not vibes

If you are building anything agent-like (tool calling, multi-step plans):

  • Maximum steps
  • Maximum wall-clock time
  • Allowlist of tools (read calendar ✗ delete calendar until proven)
  • Human confirmation for irreversible actions

Pausing / resuming agents is a hot topic for a reason: long-running autonomy without checkpoints is how you get surprise side effects. Even a simple job table with status: running | paused | done | failed beats an unbounded while-loop in memory.

Control 3: Paper trail (logs you can defend)

When someone asks "why did the assistant tell my users X?", screenshots are not enough.

Log structured events:

await db.aiEvents.insert({
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  tenantId,
  userId,
  featureKey,
  model,
  promptVersion,      // e.g. "rsvp-helper@3"
  inputHash,          // hash raw input; store raw only if policy allows
  toolCalls: [...],   // names + args summaries
  outputHash,
  tokensIn,
  tokensOut,
  latencyMs,
  createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
});

Privacy-aware defaults

  • Prefer hashes + short redacted previews over full prompts for sensitive products
  • Never log API keys, auth headers, or payment fields
  • Define retention (30/90 days) and stick to it
  • Make "export my AI history / delete my AI history" a real endpoint if you serve EU users or simply respect people

Prompt versioning is underrated

Store prompts in git (prompts/rsvp-helper.v3.md) and send promptVersion with every call. When behavior changes, you can diff. "The model got dumber" is often "we edited the prompt on Tuesday and forgot."

A thin React admin that earns its keep

You do not need a full observability suite on day one. A single authenticated page with:

  • Feature flags table + toggle
  • Today's spend / call counts per feature
  • Last 50 AI events (status, latency, error code)
  • Big red "disable all AI features" button

…will save you more pain than another model provider abstraction.

How this maps to a real feature

Suppose you add "Suggest event description" for organizers:

  1. Flag: events.ai.suggest-description (default off in prod until soak test)
  2. Budget: 20 suggestions / organizer / day, 1k max input chars
  3. Paper trail: prompt version + hashes + tokens
  4. UX: show the suggestion as a diff the human must accept — never auto-publish
  5. Kill: if suggestions degrade, flip the flag; the rest of the app keeps working

That is product engineering. The model is a dependency, not the product.

Takeaways
